what_i_got_wrong: Nothing that reached the tree, but two process notes. (1) I wrote the new ledger row with a hand-typed json.dump(indent=1) before remembering ledger_io.write_ledger is the pinned writer — it rewrote 7,353 lines of diff noise for one entry, and I re-serialised through ledger_io before staging anything. AUT-PD-037 recorded this exact hazard and I hit it anyway. (2) I started a preflight before the tree was settled and had to kill it, which §6 explicitly says to expect and to do rather than sit through — recorded because the rule earned its place by being broken, not because the kill was wrong. (3) I resolved the ledger conflict with `git checkout --theirs` first, which in a stash-pop means the STASH, not the trunk — the opposite of what I wanted, and it silently produced a 250-entry file that looked plausible. Caught by asserting the entry count against the two sides I had already read, not by noticing. `git show :2:` and `:3:` are unambiguous where --ours and --theirs invert; the file count was the only tell. (4) I applied the claim locally with claim.py and did not push it, because the row did not yet exist on the trunk. That is the AUT-PD-021 lesson exactly — an unpushed claim protects nothing — and while it did not cause the collision above (the other session filed a different item, not a contested one), the collision is what an unpushed claim looks like when it DOES bite. A new row should be created, pushed, and only then worked.

gate: ./scripts/preflight.sh, read from its own EXIT marker and not from the harness's reported code — which said 0 for a run whose marker said EXIT=1, the trap the handoff prompt names. Three runs: one killed deliberately when the tree moved under it (§6 says to do that rather than protect it); one that failed on exactly one gate, the ASO archive manifest, which is stale BY CONSTRUCTION until the tree it hashes is committed; and the final run on the tree actually pushed. ⚠ THE MANIFEST IS NECESSARILY A SEPARATE COMMIT and its intermediate commit therefore carries a stale one — the generator writes `git_tree_is_clean_apart_from_this_manifest: false` and --check REFUSES over a dirty tree, so there is no ordering in which one commit satisfies both. Recorded as the deviation it is; the green run is the one that saw the pushed tree.
